transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start off, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

I came in because I’m tired all the time. By midmorning at work, even after just reviewing files or helping a junior adjuster with a claim, it feels like my body and my brain are already running on empty.
How would you describe your sleep lately—do you feel rested when you wake up, or do you have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid close attention to my sleep specifically—I just know I’m worn out during the day.
Has anyone told you that you snore loudly or stop breathing for moments while you sleep?
I’m not sure. No one’s mentioned anything like that to me.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, or have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most of the day?

Most days, yes. It feels like there’s a gray film over everything. Even when my husband is kind or we’re cooking with the family, I go through the motions, but I don’t really feel the enjoyment I used to.
How long have you been feeling this way—down and less interested in things you used to enjoy?
About three years and three months, I think. It started around when I was moved into the higher-responsibility role at work—mentoring adjusters and overseeing the new workflow systems.
During these past three years, have there been any stretches of two months or longer when you felt essentially back to your normal self, without the low mood or loss of interest?
No, I can’t think of a two-month stretch where I felt back to normal. It’s been pretty steady since that job change about three years and three months ago.
Have you noticed any unintentional weight gain or weight loss over these past few years?
I haven’t really noticed any clear change in my weight.
Have you noticed feeling unusually cold, having dry skin, or being more constipated than usual over these past few years?
I haven’t noticed anything like that, no.
Have you noticed being unusually thirsty or needing to urinate more often than usual recently?
No, I haven’t noticed being especially thirsty or needing to go to the bathroom more often.
Have you noticed feeling unusually short of breath or lightheaded when climbing stairs or exerting yourself physically?
No, I can’t say I’ve noticed that when I’m climbing stairs or doing something physical.
Even after what seems like a full night's sleep, do you find yourself feeling excessively drowsy during the day, such as needing to nap or struggling to stay awake during quiet activities?
Yes. I’m tired all the time. By midmorning at work, even after just reviewing files or helping a junior adjuster with a claim, I feel like my body and my brain are already running on empty.
On a typical night, about how many hours of sleep do you get?
I'm not really sure—I haven't been keeping track of the hours.
Do you ever find yourself actually falling asleep unintentionally during the day—like during a meeting, while driving, or watching TV—rather than just feeling tired?
I don’t usually actually fall asleep like that. It’s more that I’m so tired by midmorning, just going through files or helping someone with a claim, that I feel completely drained.
When your alarm goes off in the morning, do you have a hard time waking up or feel very groggy and disoriented for a while afterward?

I’m pretty groggy in the morning, yes. But honestly, the tiredness just keeps going—by midmorning at work, after reviewing files or helping a junior adjuster with a claim, I already feel like I’m running on empty.
If you do take a nap during the day, does it leave you feeling refreshed and less tired afterward, or do you still feel just as exhausted?

I don’t really nap much. I just know that by midmorning, even after routine work like reviewing files or helping someone with a claim, I already feel completely drained—like my body and brain are running on empty.
Have you noticed feeling unusually guilty, worthless, or having trouble concentrating or making decisions during this time?

I’ve been having trouble concentrating, yes. At work I’m missing details in audits and taking longer to sign off on files. And outside work, I’ve pulled back from painting, hiking, and volunteering—I’m mostly just trying to get through the week.
On nights when you're not rushed by an alarm, about how many hours do you naturally sleep before waking up on your own?
I’m not really sure—I haven’t paid close attention to how many hours I sleep when I don’t have to get up for something.
On days when you don't have to work, like weekends, do you find that you sleep noticeably longer than usual—say, more than 9 or 10 hours?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really noticed whether I sleep that much longer on weekends.
Did you notice this constant tiredness and drowsiness starting before you began feeling down and losing interest in things, or did it start around the same time as those mood changes?

It started around the same time, I think. I just feel tired all the time now—by midmorning at work, even after reviewing files or helping a junior adjuster with a claim, my body and brain already feel empty.
On days when your mood feels a little better than usual, do you still notice the same level of exhaustion and drowsiness, or does the tiredness ease up along with your mood?

Even when I’m feeling a little better, I’m still exhausted. By midmorning, just reviewing files or helping a junior adjuster with a claim, it feels like my body and brain are already running on empty.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a chronic, essentially continuous depressed mood and anhedonia lasting over three years without any 2-month symptom-free interval, consistent with Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia). Associated symptoms include low energy/fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and withdrawal from previously enjoyed activities—core criteria for dysthymia. While the patient reports significant daytime tiredness and grogginess, she denies unintentional sleep episodes, cannot quantify sleep duration or confirm long weekend sleep (>9-10 hrs), and the fatigue persists in parallel with mood symptoms rather than as an independent, primary sleep-wake disturbance. This makes an independent Hypersomnolence Disorder (F51.11) diagnosis less supported, as the fatigue appears better explained as a vegetative/somatic feature of the persistent depressive disorder rather than a distinct primary sleep disorder with restorative sleep architecture disruption. No evidence of medical (thyroid, diabetes, sleep apnea) or manic/hypomanic episodes was found, and no discrete major depressive episodes with clear remission periods were identified, further supporting dysthymia over episodic MDD or a primary sleep disorder.
